passages.t: A lily among thorns, and the first charge
passages.happening:
‘I am a rose of Sharon, a lily of the valley’ (verse 1), she says. He answers, ‘Like a lily among the thorns is my darling among the maidens’ (verse 2). She replies, ‘Like an apple tree among the trees of the forest is my beloved among the young men’ (verse 3). She delights to sit in his shade.

‘He has brought me to the house of wine, and his banner over me is love’ (verse 4). She asks to be refreshed with raisins and apples, for she is faint with love (verse 5), and she rests in his embrace (verse 6).

Then the first of three charges: “O daughters of Jerusalem, I adjure you by the gazelles and does of the field: Do not arouse or awaken love until the time is right” (verse 7).
passages.hearers:
The rose of Sharon and the lily of the valley were probably common wildflowers, not garden roses and lilies; the first may have been a crocus. Sharon was the fertile coastal plain known for its pastures and flowers. She may be modestly calling herself an ordinary flower of the field, and he answers that she is a lily among thorns. The ‘apple tree’ may be an apple, an apricot or a quince. Raisin cakes were a festive food. Lovesickness, a longing so strong it makes one faint, is a theme in Egyptian love poetry too.

A banner was a standard carried over a company. His banner over her is love.

The charge in verse 7 is an oath, but instead of swearing by God it swears by graceful wild animals. Many scholars note that the Hebrew words for gazelles and does of the field sound like two names of God, the LORD of Hosts and God Almighty, and suggest a deliberate play that avoids using God's name in a love poem.
passages.later: Isaiah speaks of Sharon's flowering: ‘the splendor of Carmel and Sharon’ (Isaiah 35:2). And the raisin cakes of verse 5 were festive food: David gave them to the people when the ark came to Jerusalem (2 Samuel 6:19).
passages.hard:
What does the charge not to arouse or awaken love until the time is right mean?

The refrain comes three times (2:7; 3:5; 8:4), each time after a scene of closeness, and interpreters understand it in several ways.

Many readers, Jewish and Christian, have taken it as a call to patience and chastity. Love has great power, and its full expression should wait for the right time and setting, which the Song and the rest of Scripture place in marriage. Others read the Hebrew as until it pleases, a request not to disturb the lovers until their love has run its course. Still others hear general wisdom about love's power: it should not be forced, manipulated or stirred up artificially.

These readings are not exclusive, and the refrain's place after moments of closeness suggests that love's timing matters. The woman who speaks the charge is not ashamed of desire. She knows that it is strong enough to be handled with care. And on every reading, love in the Song is freely given. Nothing here gives anyone a right to press or force another.
passages.asks: Love is strong enough to be handled with care. Ask whether you have tried to hurry love, or to stir it up before its time. And ask how you can honor the freedom of the person you love, never pressing them.

passages.t: Arise, come away: the winter is past
passages.happening:
“Listen! My beloved approaches. Look! Here he comes, leaping across the mountains, bounding over the hills” (verse 8). He is like a gazelle or a young stag, and he stands behind the wall, looking through the lattice (verse 9).

He calls her: “Arise, my darling. Come away with me, my beautiful one. For now the winter is past; the rain is over and gone” (verses 10-11). ‘The flowers have appeared in the countryside; the season of singing has come, and the cooing of turtledoves is heard in our land’ (verse 12). The figs are ripening and the vines are in bloom (verse 13).

‘O my dove in the clefts of the rock, in the crevices of the cliff, let me see your face, let me hear your voice’ (verse 14). Someone asks for the little foxes that ruin the vineyards to be caught (verse 15).

“My beloved is mine and I am his; he pastures his flock among the lilies” (verse 16). And she asks him to turn, like a gazelle on the mountains, until the day breaks (verse 17).
passages.hearers:
This scene fits the land's own spring. The winter rains end around March or April, wildflowers cover the hills, fig trees put out early fruit, and migrating turtledoves return. His invitation is framed by the repeated call, arise, come away, a small love song set in spring.

Little foxes were a real threat to vineyards, digging and eating the grapes. The saying may picture any small danger that could spoil a budding love.

Verse 16 is the first of the Song's three statements of mutual belonging (compare 6:3 and 7:10). The mountains of Bether in verse 17 are hard to identify; the word may name a place or mean divided, rugged hills.
passages.later: The prophets used the same picture of a wild doe for strength and freedom: ‘He makes my feet like those of a deer’ (Habakkuk 3:19). And a psalm longs for a dove's freedom: “Oh, that I had wings like a dove! I would fly away and find rest” (Psalm 55:6).
passages.asks: The lovers belong to each other. Ask what small foxes, little habits or neglects, could spoil a love you treasure. And ask how you could give someone you love the gift of a new season, an invitation to come away and rest.
